messages.subject: Re: [Rqtl-disc] Question on plots of recomb freq and lod
messages.subject_clean: [Rqtl-disc] Question on plots of recomb freq and lod
messages.body_plain:
Thanks; I was simply looking for a way to calculate summary statistics about recombination rates. I think I found how to obtain the information we needed using the est.map to convert our prior physical-distance map to one in cM, and then taking that estimate of genetic distance (chromosome length in cM) divided by physical distance (Megabases) to yield a recombination rate for the chromosome. We're working with insects and I just used the Haldane map function; if I recall for this purpose map function wouldn't matter much.

I was wondering about taking column averages from the pull.rf() as a way to convert from a pairwise recombination rate, to an average recombination rate for each marker. So far I've just ended up taking cM/Mb, or, I think equivalently (values are very close albeit not exactly the same), computing:
(100 * output of count.xo) / (total # of individuals) = recombination rate in cM/Mb.
Thanks again,
Hilary

On Thursday, January 31, 2013 9:37:16 AM UTC-5, Karl Broman wrote:
>
> On Jan 28, 2013, at 10:25 AM, HASmith <hasmith...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> > Hi,
> > I'm trying to use rqtl to assess recombination frequency. Yet when I use the plotRF function, I know that red = high lod score & low recombination frequency, but what is the scale (i.e., what cutoffs/numeric thresholds are used to define red, blue, etc.)?
>
> The scale is relatively arbitrary.  We threshold the high LOD scores (argument zmax, with default value 10) and transform the recombination fractions to be on a similar scale (with the formula   -4*(log2(rf) + 1)/12 * zmax ).
>
>
> > For me an even better result would be perhaps if it were possible to generate a plot showing all markers on the x-axis, and the recombination frequency on the y-axis. I found a somewhat similar function described in an online rqtl guide to mapping (rf <- pull.rf(mapthis); lod <- pull.rf(mapthis, what="lod"); plot(as.numeric(rf), as.numeric(lod), xlab="Recombination fraction", ylab="LOD score"). Yet as this is plotting against lod score, it's not quite what I need. The closest I came up with was to use write.csv to save the "rf" matrix to a file, then take the average down each column for a value of the recombination frequency at that marker. Does this sound correct, or is there a better way? Sorry if it's a somewhat basic question.
>
> I'm not sure what you're trying to look at.  There is an estimated recombination fraction and LOD score for every pair of markers.  The code you cite, using pull.rf(), pulls out the two things as two separate square matrices, with rows and columns corresponding to markers.  But I'm not sure why you'd be interested in the column averages.
>
> karl

messages.body_plain:
If your interest is in estimating recombination rates, I don't see how the pairwise recombination fractions from est.rf will be of any use to you.

My package R/xoi includes a function est.recrate() that uses a genetic map and physical map of a chromosome to get a smoothed estimated of recombination rate along the chromosome.

  https://github.com/kbroman/xoi
  http://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/xoi/

karl

messages.subject: Re: [Rqtl-disc] 2-QTL scans sapping memory/giving amazing LOD scores
messages.subject_clean: [Rqtl-disc] 2-QTL scans sapping memory/giving amazing LOD scores
messages.body_plain:
scantwo requires a great deal of memory, especially, as in your case, with a very large number of markers.

Regarding the extremely large LOD scores, such things generally occur in the case of outliers in the phenotype, or a highly skewed phenotype distribution.  I would focus on Haley-Knott regression (method="hk").

karl

messages.subject: Genetic map estimation does not converge for dense marker set
messages.subject_clean: Genetic map estimation does not converge for dense marker set
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I'm trying to estimate the genetic map for a data set of haploid
individuals. After about 24 hours of computation with the read.cross
command (no genetic or physical distances are included in the input
file) I get this message:

    --Read the following data:
             172  individuals
             52466  markers
             13  phenotypes
     --Estimating genetic map
     --Cross type: bc
    Warning messages:
    1: Didn't converge!
    2: Didn't converge!
    3: In summary.cross(cross) :
      Some chromosomes > 1000 cM in length; there may be a problem
with the genetic map.
      (Perhaps it is in basepairs?)

I don't know the large number of markers that I have makes the
computation problematic? Maybe one can tweak the parameters of the map
estimation?

On the other hand, I'm thinking that since my marker set is so dense
(one marker every ~250 bp on average) and I have very little missing
data maybe I'm as good off with simple marker regression (for which I
assume a genetic map is not used). I'm not fully read up on the more
sophisticated methods implemented in rQTL, but my feeling is that a
lot of the juice in those methods goes into more accurately locating
QTLs when you have sparse markers and   potentially a lot of missing
genotype data?

messages.subject: Re: [Rqtl-disc] Genetic map estimation does not converge for dense marker set
messages.subject_clean: [Rqtl-disc] Genetic map estimation does not converge for dense marker set
messages.body_plain:
If you don't provide marker positions but just chromosome IDs, read.cross will attempt to infer inter-marker distances, which can take a very long time.

I would use read.cross with estimate.map=FALSE.  The markers will be assigned arbitrary genetic map locations, but you'll be able to work on estimating the map afterwards.

If you have physical positions for the markers, it's best to include them in the file, but on a Mbp scale rather than bp scale, and even better would be to use what knowledge you have of recombination rate to assign estimated genetic map positions to markers.

karl

messages.subject: Additive Effect Estimation with SG
messages.body_plain:
Karl:

I would like to get your insight/comments on the estimation of additive effects in Rqtl when one has (like I do) a selectively genotyped (50 Highest / 50 Lowest Phenotype) plant population of 264 RILs.

With SG you get purposeful (systematic) missing genotypes, as opposed to (say) random missing genotypes in a (mostly) fully genotyped population.  Multiple imputation is the obvious choice with the latter scenario, but what about  an SG scenario?

The reason I ask this question is that I am now working with Rqtl commands to get additive effect estimates (and graphs thereof) of just the single (only) major QTL LOD score peak that I detected on Chr 7.

Multiple imputation (via sim.geno) is automatically invoked in (most) of those Rqtl cmds (such as effectscan, effectplot, fitqtl) and result in AA : BB RIL means of 3.21 : 2.81 for the SNP tightly linked to this Chr 7 QTL.  The additive effect is estimated to be -0.17 using fitqtl with the parameter what=”draws”.

Without imputation, the graph I get when  using the plot.pxg cmd (with the parameter infer=FALSE) displays SNP AA : BB means of 3.37 : 2.48, which would infer an additive effect of (3.37-2.48)/2= -0.44.  In fact, the estimate of -0.40 was obtained using fitqtl with the parameter what=”prob”, which is a Haley-Knott regression estimate, but does not HK perform poorly with missing data (as in an SG pop)?

Is there an max likelihood (EM) option (with calc.prob) for computing additive effects in SG pops?  In any case, I would greatly appreciate your insight on the add effect estimate one should report when using SG.

Thanks!

Jim

messages.subject: Re: [Rqtl-disc] Additive Effect Estimation with SG
messages.body_plain:
R/qtl doesn't currently have code to get MLEs of additive effects; only Haley-Knott regression or multiple imputation.

In the case of selective genotyping, Haley-Knott is really bad, so you're only option is imputation.
You want to be sure to include data on all phenotyped individuals and not just those with genotypes.

karl

karl

messages.subject: Re: [Rqtl-disc] Coding phase for outcross using 4way cross format?
messages.subject_clean: [Rqtl-disc] Coding phase for outcross using 4way cross format?
messages.body_plain:
> Given this outcross design, there can be up to 4 alleles at a given marker, and segregation types include "intercross", "backcross", 3allele and 4 allele.  I would like to include all of the segregation types in one analysis, so I am trying to work out how this can be done within the 4way format.  In particular, my question centers on how phase is encoded in the AB x CD form.  Perhaps this is described somewhere, but I couldn't find it in the help for read.cross or in the book.

The only documentation is in the help file for read.cross, but it's just one line on the numeric codes for the possible genotypes.

> In the absence of any real knowledge, I've worked out the following scheme-- the next 3 paragraphs will reveal whether I've got it or not.  If not, could you steer me to the correct way to encode phase, and let me know if I can code all the segregation types in the 4way format?
>
> Starting with the help file for read.cross:
> "For a 4-way cross, the mother and father are assumed to have genotypes AB and CD, respectively”
> Do I understand correctly that the “mother and father” are the two F1 genotypes, making their progeny the F2?  This would mean the original parentals are AC and BD?

It's easiest to think of a two crosses involving four inbred lines, AA x BB and CC x DD.

The F1 would then be AB and CD.

You can use this for a cross between two outbred individuals, provided that you can reconstruct phase in the two F1 individuals (the parents of the four-way cross progeny.

> The genotype data for the progeny is assumed to be phase-known,
> Is phase encoded by the position within the cross AB x CD?  If  we always keep the F1 genotypes in this order, then alleles A and C are from P1 (genotype AC) while B and D are from P2 (BD)?

No, really I'm thinking of the F1s as two individuals with completely different parents.

> If this is true, then I think that any segregation pattern (backcross, intercross, 3 alleles)  could be coded with the appropriate phase (which I already know) by arranging alleles from the two parents in the AB x CD format.  In this scheme whatever alleles we put in the A and C position came from P1, while alleles in the B and D positions came from P2.  If this is dead wrong, no need to read further!  If it has potential, I've worked out several examples.

You need to work out phase, which means determining the relationship between alleles at different markers. For example, if you have two markers that are GT one parent and TT in the other, you need to figure out whether the G's go together or the T's.

karl
